translation: Two other small pictures with scalloped edges, presumably from the same year, show the same child, but smaller, in a dress with flounces and balloon sleeves.
In the first one, she mischievously snuggles up against a large-bodied woman, solid in a broadly striped dress, with her hair twisted up in large rolls.
On the other, she raises her left fist, the right one held back by a tall man in a light jacket and creased trousers, striking a nonchalant pose.
The two photos were taken on the same day in front of a low wall topped with a border of flowers, in a paved courtyard.
Above their heads a clothesline passes by, on which a pin has remained hooked.

Another photo, signed by the same photographer but with more ordinary booklet paper and the gold border gone likely destined for the same family distribution, shows a little girl of about four years old, serious, almost sad despite a good chubby face beneath short hair, parted in the middle and pulled back by barrettes to which are attached ribbons like butterflies.
The left hand rests on the same fully visible, Louis XVI style carved table.
She appears plump in her blouse, her pinafore skirt raised at the front due to a prominent belly, perhaps a sign of rickets (around 1944).
The boys were proud to join the regiment and people thought they looked handsome in uniform.
On the evening of the conscription board, they would go bar hopping to celebrate the glory of being recognized as real men.
Before joining the regiment, they were just kids and had no value in the labor and marriage market.
Afterwards, they could have a wife and children.
The uniform they paraded around the neighborhood during their leaves swathed them in patriotic beauty and virtual sacrifice.
The shadow of the victorious fighters, the GIs, hung around them.
The coarse cloth of the uniform, brushed against when one stood on tiptoe to kiss them, embodied the absolute divide between the world of men and that of women.
Looking at them, one felt a sense of heroism.

Under the unchanging scene, the circus posters from last year with Roger Lanzac's photo, the first communion pictures given to friends, the Songwriters' Club on Radio Luxembourg, the days were filled with new desires.
On Sunday afternoons, everyone would crowd against the general electric store's window to watch the television.
Cafes were investing in buying a station to attract customers.
On the flank of the hills, motocross tracks snaked and one watched the deafening vehicles go up and down all day long.
The growing impatience of commerce with its new watchwords, "initiative", "dynamism", was shaking up the routine of the cities.
Between the fair and the festival, the Commercial Fortnight established itself as a springtime ritual.
In the downtown streets, loudspeakers blared out appeals to buy, interspersed with songs by Annie Cordy and Eddie Constantine, to win the Simca or the dining room set.

On the podium, at the town hall square, a local host was making people laugh with jokes from Roger Nicolas and Jean Richard, gathering contestants for Sing or Sink and Double or Quits, just like on the radio.
Seated in a corner of the podium, the Queen of Commerce sat enthroned under her crown.
The merchandise moved forward in festive colors.
People were saying "things change" or "we mustn't stagnate, it's dull to stay at home".
But they only spoke of what they had seen, which could be relived by eating and drinking.
They lacked the talent or conviction to talk about what they knew but had not seen.
So neither of Jewish children getting on trains for Auschwitz, nor of the starving dead collected in the morning in the Warsaw Ghetto, nor of the 10,000 degrees at Hiroshima.

Hence this impression that history classes, documentaries and films wouldn't dispel later: neither the crematoriums nor the atomic bomb were in the same era as black market butter, air raid warnings and trips to the basement.
They segued by comparison into discussing the previous war, the Great one, that of '14, which was won amidst blood and glory, a man's war which the women at the table listened to with respect.
They talked about the Chemin des Dames and Verdun, about those gassed, about the bells of November 11, 1918.
They named villages from which not a single child who had gone to the front had returned.
They contrasted the soldiers in the muddy trenches with the well-sheltered prisoners of 40, who had been warm and safe for five years without even having bombs dropped on them.
They were arguing over heroism and misfortune.

The children weren't listening and hurried to leave the table as soon as they had been given permission, taking advantage of the general goodwill on holidays to engage in forbidden games, jump on beds, and swing upside down.
But they kept everything.

Beside the fabulous time, of which they would not order the episodes for a long time The Debacle, The Exodus, The Occupation, The Landing, The Victorythey found their unnamed present one in which they were growing up quite dull.
They regretted not having been born, or barely so, when it was necessary to go off in a troop on the roads and sleep on straw like gypsies.
They would hold on to the deep regret of this unlived time.
The memories of others passed on to them a secret nostalgia for a time they had barely missed and the hope of experiencing it one day.
The frenzy that had followed the Liberation was fading.
So, people could only think about going out and the world was full of desires to be satisfied on the spot.
Everything that was a first since the war caused a stampede, bananas, national lottery tickets, fireworks.

Whole neighborhoods, from the grandmother led by her daughters to the infant in its pram, were rushing to the fair, to the torchlight procession, to Bouglione's circus where they were nearly trampled in the crush.
They flocked in a praying and singing crowd to the road to welcome the statue of Our Lady of Boulogne and accompany her for miles the next day.
Secular or religious, any occasion was a good reason for them to be outside together, as if they wanted to continue living collectively.
On Sunday evenings, the buses returned from the sea with tall young men in shorts singing at the top of their lungs, perched on the luggage rack.
The dogs roamed freely and mated in the middle of the street.
Family stories and social narratives are one and the same.

The voices of the guests laid out the realms of youth: the countryside and farms where, in lost memory, men were appointed and girls were maids, the factory where they had all encountered each other, socialized and married, small businesses where the most ambitious had succeeded.

They sketched out stories with no personal events other than births, marriages, and mourning, without travels outside of the regiment to a distant garrison town, existences occupied by work, its harshness and its wear, the threats of drink.
The school was a mythical backdrop, a brief golden age with the Teacher as its harsh god wielding his iron ruler to rap on knuckles.
From hand to hand went faded photos, their backs marked by all the fingers that had held them at other meals, a mixture of coffee and grease blended into an indescribable color.
In the solemn and stiff newlyweds, the wedding guests lined up in several rows along a wall, one could not recognize either their relatives or anyone else.
It wasn't oneself either that one saw in the half-naked, gender-indistinct baby on a cushion but someone else, a creature belonging to a silent and inaccessible time.
